h1: Beer with Kerala sadya and other South Indian vegetarian feasts
title: Beer with a Kerala Sadya | Craft Beer School
desc: How to pair beer with a Kerala sadya and other South Indian vegetarian feasts: sambar, avial, olan, thoran, pickles and payasam.
teaser: A sadya is two dozen dishes on one banana leaf. One well chosen beer can handle most of them.
standfirst: A Kerala sadya puts sweet, sour, salty, bitter and hot on the same leaf at once. Matching a beer to every dish is impossible, so the trick is to choose one that refreshes across the whole meal. Here is how we would do it.
sections: A sadya is a whole meal on one leaf

The sadya is the great vegetarian feast of Kerala, served on a banana leaf at Onam, Vishu and weddings. A full sadya can have more than twenty items: rice, parippu (dal) with ghee, sambar, rasam, avial, olan, thoran, erissery, kalan, pachadi, kichadi, pickles, banana chips, sharkara varatti, pappadam and several kinds of payasam.

The dishes are not eaten one at a time like courses. You mix them with rice in an order that families argue about. So a sadya beer has to be a generalist: something that refreshes after sour, sweet and spicy alike.

A note before the pairings: at many homes and temples, a sadya is a religious or family occasion where alcohol has no place. Respect that. These suggestions are for a sadya style meal at home or a restaurant where beer is welcome.
Coconut is the thread through the meal

Coconut runs through most sadya dishes. Avial mixes vegetables with coconut and yoghurt, finished with coconut oil and curry leaves. Olan is white pumpkin and cowpeas in coconut milk. Thoran is a dry stir fry with grated coconut. Erissery adds roasted coconut to pumpkin and beans.

Coconut is fatty and slightly sweet. A Belgian witbier is the best single match we know: its wheat body suits the creaminess, while its orange peel and coriander seed brighten the coconut. It is usually brewed at 4.5 to 5.5% ABV with low bitterness, around 10 to 20 IBU, which keeps it friendly to the sour and spicy dishes too.
Sambar, rasam and the sour dishes

Sambar and rasam bring tamarind sourness, while rasam adds black pepper heat. Kalan and pulissery are yoghurt based and sour. Puli inji, a sweet, sour and hot ginger tamarind relish, packs a lot into a small spoonful.

Sour food makes very bitter beers taste harsh, so this is another reason to avoid an IPA at a sadya. A crisp lager, a Kölsch or the witbier will refresh. A gose, slightly salty and tart, is an interesting match with pulissery if you want to experiment.

Mango and lime pickles are salty, sour and hot. Banana chips fried in coconut oil and crisp pappadam are pure crunch and salt. These are the most beer friendly items on the leaf.

A Pilsner at 25 to 40 IBU is excellent with pappadam and chips, its bitterness and carbonation cutting the coconut oil. With the pickles, stick to the lower bitterness beers. If you are pouring one beer for the whole sadya, the witbier still covers these well. Our guide to beer with South Indian food has more on coconut oil frying.

Bitter dishes need a word. Pavakka (bitter gourd) appears at some sadyas, as a fry or in a theeyal. Bitter food and bitter beer pile up, so a highly hopped beer makes bitter gourd taste harsher still. Soft malt helps. A Helles or the witbier is the kinder choice.

The sadya ends with payasam, often two or more kinds. Ada pradhaman is made with rice flakes, jaggery and coconut milk. Palada is a milk payasam with rice flakes. Parippu pradhaman uses lentils and jaggery.

Sweet desserts make most beers taste thin and bitter. If you want a beer with payasam, choose one at least as sweet as the dish, such as a milk stout or a sweet stout at 4 to 6% ABV. Jaggery and coconut sit nicely beside the beer's chocolate and coffee notes. Otherwise, finish the beer before the payasam arrives.

Tamil Nadu's wedding meals on a banana leaf, Karnataka's oota and Andhra's bhojanam follow a similar pattern with regional differences. Tamil meals bring kootu, poriyal and more rasam. Udupi meals favour sweet notes and gojju. Andhra meals add gunpowder podi, ghee and hotter pickles.

The approach stays the same. Pick one versatile, low bitterness beer for the whole leaf. Witbier is the all rounder. A Helles or a Kölsch is the lighter option. For hotter Andhra meals, a hefeweizen. Serve all of these cold, 4 to 7 °C, which also helps on a warm Kerala afternoon. Our Indian food and beer pairing guide covers regional heat levels in more depth.

A good way to understand this is to try two beers across one sadya style plate: a witbier and an IPA. Taste each with avial, sambar, pickle and pappadam. The IPA may shine with the pappadam but struggle with the sambar and pickle. The witbier will rarely be the best match for any single dish, yet it will be good with almost all of them. That is what a feast beer needs to do.

Your first step: next time you have a South Indian vegetarian meal where beer is welcome, pour a witbier and taste it with three different dishes on the leaf. Note which dish it suits best and which it suits least.
faqs: What beer goes with a Kerala sadya?
A Belgian witbier is the best all rounder. Its wheat body suits coconut dishes, its citrus brightens the meal and its low bitterness handles sour and spicy items.
Is beer appropriate at a sadya?
Often not. Many sadyas are religious or family occasions where alcohol has no place. These pairings are for sadya style meals where beer is welcome.
A milk stout or sweet stout, at least as sweet as the payasam. Most other beers taste thin and bitter next to jaggery desserts.
